videos.title: The Tube strike that made commutes faster
videos.hook: In February 2014, a strike closed 171 of London's 270 Tube stations.
videos.caption: In February 2014 a strike closed 171 of London's 270 Tube stations, and about 1 in 20 disrupted commuters kept the new, faster route. What are you still doing only because it's good enough? #london #behaviouraleconomics #decisionmaking
videos.core_claim: People stop searching once a routine is good enough; a 2014 Tube strike forced London commuters to try new routes and about 5% of those disrupted kept a faster one, saving ~400 seconds per trip.
videos.concept_key: forced disruption of a routine > under-experimentation revealed > better option found only when the old one broke

videos.title: Hertz's EV sell-off
videos.hook: In January 2024, Hertz said it would sell about 20,000 of its electric cars.
videos.caption: Hertz announced plans to buy 100,000 Teslas in 2021, then in January 2024 said it would sell about 20,000 EVs and take a $245M hit. For a rental company, the price of the car it will sell later is part of the cost.
videos.core_claim: A rental company's cost of a car is purchase price minus resale value, so Tesla's 2023 price cuts on new EVs cut the value of Hertz's fleet and helped force a 20,000-EV sell-off with a ~$245M depreciation charge.
videos.concept_key: owning an asset whose value is set by a supplier's pricing > supplier price cuts devalue the fleet > forced sell-off and depreciation charge

videos.title: Adobe's cancellation fee: the fee vs. the lock
videos.hook: In March 2026, Adobe agreed to a $150 million settlement over its subscriptions.
videos.caption: Adobe says early termination fees were under 0.5% of its revenue. The bigger value was the 12-month commitment behind a monthly price; in March 2026 Adobe agreed to a $150M U.S. settlement over its subscription terms.
videos.first_comment: IR-005 · Sources: DOJ release 13 Mar 2026; U.S. v. Adobe complaint (N.D. Cal. 2024); Adobe statement Jul 2024 (The Register)
videos.angle: Hidden mechanism behind a pricing/contract structure
videos.core_claim: Adobe's 'annual, paid monthly' plan shows a lower monthly price ($54.99 vs $82.49) but is a 12-month contract; cancelling in year one costs 50% of the remaining payments. Adobe says the fees were <0.5% of revenue, so the value is the 12-month commitment the fee enforces, not the fee income.
videos.concept_key: discounted monthly price that is really an annual contract > early termination fee enforces the commitment > fee income tiny, retention is the value

videos.title: HP's ink lock-in: the printer vs. the ink
videos.hook: In January 2024, HP's CEO said some of his own customers are a bad investment.
videos.tiktok_title: HP calls its own customers a 'bad investment'
videos.caption: HP's CEO said customers who skip HP's own ink are a 'bad investment' — the company prices printers near cost and makes its money on supplies, which brought in $10.9B in FY2025 alone.
videos.first_comment: IR-006 · Sources: CNBC interview Jan 2024 (Lores quote, The Register); HP Dynamic Security policy; HP FY2025 Q4 results (Nov 2025)
videos.angle: Hidden mechanism behind a hardware/consumables pricing structure
videos.core_claim: HP prices printer hardware near cost and recovers profit through high-margin ink/toner supplies ($10.9B in FY2025 alone), enforced by Dynamic Security firmware that can block non-HP or refilled cartridges — the CEO's own 'bad investment' framing describes customers who don't buy into the supplies side.
videos.concept_key: hardware sold near cost > profit recovered via locked recurring consumables > firmware enforces the lock

videos.title: The credit card that cost JPMorgan $300M
videos.hook: In December 2016, JPMorgan's CEO said a single credit card would cost the bank up to $300 million that quarter.
videos.tiktok_title: The credit card that cost JPMorgan $300M
videos.caption: In December 2016 JPMorgan's CEO said one new credit card would cost the bank up to $300M that quarter — the Chase Sapphire Reserve was so popular the bank ran out of the metal to make it, and cut the signup bonus in half the next year.
videos.first_comment: IR-007 · Sources: Bloomberg (Dimon, 6 Dec 2016); CNBC (Dimon, 18 Jan 2017); Chase Sapphire Reserve launch press release (Aug 2016)
videos.angle: Hidden mechanism behind a customer-acquisition cost decision
videos.core_claim: The Chase Sapphire Reserve's rich signup bonus and travel credit were so popular that actual customer-acquisition costs exceeded JPMorgan's projections, forcing a disclosed $200-300M hit to Q4 2016 profit — a product succeeding by exactly the metric it was designed on can still break the budget it was priced against.
videos.concept_key: promotional incentive priced against expected uptake > uptake far exceeds projection > true acquisition cost blows the budget

videos.title: The $1.72 monopoly tax on your concert ticket
videos.hook: In April 2026, a jury found Live Nation and Ticketmaster ran an illegal monopoly.
videos.tiktok_title: The $1.72 monopoly tax on your concert ticket
videos.caption: In April 2026 a jury found Live Nation and Ticketmaster ran an illegal monopoly, overcharging fans about $1.72 a ticket at major venues — by paying venues upfront and threatening to pull Live Nation shows if they booked a rival ticketer.
videos.first_comment: IR-008 · Sources: DOJ v. Live Nation complaint (23 May 2024); CNN/NBC jury verdict coverage (Apr 2026); R Street Institute case analysis
videos.core_claim: Live Nation used upfront payments (the carrot) and the threat of withholding its own tour bookings (the stick) to coerce venues into exclusive multiyear Ticketmaster contracts, removing fans' ability to shop for ticketing fees — a jury found this an illegal monopoly that overcharged fans by about $1.72/ticket at major venues.
videos.concept_key: vertical integration across promotion/venues/ticketing > exclusive contracts coerced via carrot-and-stick > no substitutable competition for the ticket buyer

videos.title: Netflix charged for passwords. Then gained 9M subscribers.
videos.hook: In 2022, Netflix said over 100 million households were sharing passwords for free.
videos.tiktok_title: Netflix charged for passwords. Then gained 9M subscribers.
videos.caption:
Netflix's own CEO said in 2016 that password sharing was something "you have to learn to live with" — years before the 2023 reversal that added millions of subscribers.

#PasswordSharing #Netflix #Streaming #BusinessCaseStudy
videos.first_comment: IR-009 · Sources: Netflix Q3 2023 earnings call (Spencer Neumann, CNBC); Netflix Q3 2016 earnings call (Reed Hastings, CNBC)
videos.angle: Counterintuitive result: the customer-unfriendly move outperformed the generous one
videos.core_claim: Netflix disclosed in 2022 that 100M+ households were sharing passwords for free; despite warnings the May 2023 paid-sharing crackdown would drive users away, it added ~9M paying subscribers in Q3 2023 alone, and CFO Spencer Neumann called it the company's primary revenue accelerator that year.
videos.concept_key: free, tolerated behavior treated as generous > monetizing it directly contradicts the 'customer-friendly' instinct > the paid version outperforms the free one

videos.title: Klarna's 'interest-free' plan isn't free. Merchants pay 6%.
videos.hook: Klarna markets its Pay in 4 plan as completely interest-free for shoppers.
videos.tiktok_title: Klarna's 'interest-free' plan isn't free. Merchants pay 6%.
videos.caption:
Klarna went public in September 2025 at a $15 billion valuation — right as it disclosed exactly how much of that value comes from merchant fees, not shopper interest.

#BuyNowPayLater #Klarna #Fintech #BusinessCaseStudy
videos.first_comment: IR-011 · Sources: Klarna Group F-1/424B4 SEC filing (2025 IPO prospectus); CNBC IPO coverage (10 Sep 2025); Motley Fool interchange fee data
videos.angle: Hidden mechanism: a 'free' consumer feature is paid for, invisibly, by a different party
videos.core_claim: Klarna markets its no-interest 'Pay in 4' plan as free for shoppers, but merchants pay Klarna up to ~5.99% per sale for it (vs. roughly 2% for a typical credit card) — merchant fees made up 57% of Klarna's total revenue in 2024, disclosed in its September 2025 IPO filing.
videos.concept_key: a service marketed as free to the consumer > the real cost is shifted to a different party (the merchant) at a multiple of the standard rate > that shifted cost becomes the company's largest revenue source
videos.gate_breakdown: Novelty 9 (fresh, from Klarna's own Sept 2025 IPO filing), Specificity 9 (named fee percentages, named revenue share, named filing), Curiosity 9 ('free' checkout that isn't), Clarity 8, Emotional tension 7 (relatable — most viewers have used BNPL), Intellectual value 8, Retention 8, Niche fit 10, Source evidence 9 (Klarna's own SEC F-1/424B4 registration statement, a primary source), Difference 9 (fintech/BNPL, distinct from IR-009's streaming and IR-010's airline/co-brand stories)
